egg-white-omelet-scrambled-or-fried-with.title: Egg white, omelet, scrambled, or fried, with cheese and meat

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of egg white prepared as an omelet, scrambled, or fried, with added cheese and meat. Egg white is a low‑calorie source of protein, while cheese and meat provide rich flavor and additional nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg white contains virtually no fat or carbs but is high in protein.
Cheese adds calcium and vitamin D, as well as a creamy texture.
Meat supplies iron, zinc, and vitamin B12, essential for blood formation and nervous system function.
The dish can be prepared quickly, making it popular for breakfasts and sports nutrition.
Different cheeses (cheddar, mozzarella, feta) change the flavor profile and nutritional content.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Egg white provides about 10 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: Without the yolk, the dish contains minimal saturated fat, which is beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese contributes a significant amount of calcium, supporting bone and tooth health.

items.title: Iron and vitamin B12 from meat
items.content: Meat offers easily absorbable iron and vitamin B12, important for energy and nerve function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The absence of carbohydrates makes the dish suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg white.

items.title: Sodium content in cheese and meat
items.content: Cheeses and processed meats are often high in salt, which can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Processed meat products
items.content: If using sausages or bacon, consider the presence of preservatives and saturated fats.

items.title: Potential food toxins
items.content: Undercooked egg white may contain biologically active compounds that cause digestive upset.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Whisk the egg white, add diced cheese and finely chopped meat (ham, chicken, turkey). Cook in a lightly oiled pan: for an omelet – until golden, for scrambled – stir continuously, for fried – quickly sear both sides. Serve hot.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 1 month. Thaw in the fridge, then reheat in a pan or microwave.

content.title: About
content.content: Raw salmon is the flesh of Atlantic or Pacific salmon from the family Salmonidae, usually sold as boneless, skinless fillets. It has a delicate pink color, soft texture, and a characteristic sea‑like aroma. Raw salmon is commonly used in sushi, sashimi, marinades, and cold appetizers.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Salmon is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids EPA and DHA, which are important for cardiovascular health.
Wild salmon typically has a brighter color and more intense flavor than farm‑raised fish.
In Japan the fish is called “sake,” while in Scandinavia it is known as “lax.”
Salmon can change flesh color depending on diet; carotenoids from shrimp and plankton give it a pink hue.
In Japan salmon is considered a symbol of good luck and is often served at celebrations.

items.title: Rich source of omega‑3
items.content: Omega‑3 fatty acids support heart health, reduce inflammation, and aid brain function.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Raw salmon provides a complete set of essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains B12, B6 and niacin, which are involved in energy metabolism and nervous system support.

items.title: Selenium and vitamin D
items.content: Selenium acts as a powerful antioxidant, while vitamin D is essential for bone health and immunity.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with red meat, salmon has less saturated fat, making it a more heart‑friendly protein source.

items.title: Parasite risk
items.content: Raw fish may harbor Anisakis, Opisthorchis and other parasites; freezing fillets at –20 °C for at least 7 days is recommended before consumption.

items.title: Mercury and heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Larger specimens can accumulate mercury; pregnant women and children should limit intake.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions ranging from skin rash to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium in cured salmon
items.content: If the salmon is already cured or smoked, consume it in moderation to avoid excess salt.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw salmon is sliced thin for sashimi, used in rolls, marinated in soy sauce with lemon or vinegar, added to salads and cold appetizers. It is often served chilled at about 5 °C.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw salmon in an airtight container on the coldest refrigerator shelf (0–2 °C) for up to 2 days. For longer storage freeze at –18 °C, where it retains quality for up to 3 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Green tea is a drink made from the leaves of the tea plant Camellia sinensis that are not oxidized: after harvest they are quickly heated. It has a fresh, grassy, slightly bitter flavor and a pale green or golden brew. Green tea is drunk hot or iced and is also made into matcha powder.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green and black tea come from the same plant, but green tea is not oxidized.
In Japan the leaves are usually steamed, while in China they are often pan-fired.
Matcha is a powder of finely ground leaves grown in the shade.
Well-known green teas include sencha, Longjing, and gyokuro.
Green tea is best brewed with water that is not boiling, at about 70–80 °C.

items.title: Contains catechins
items.content: Catechins, including EGCG, are antioxidants that are actively studied.

items.title: Contains L-theanine
items.content: This amino acid together with caffeine may promote calm focus.

items.title: Contains a moderate amount of caffeine
items.content: Green tea usually has less caffeine than coffee, and it supports alertness.

items.title: Contains flavonoids
items.content: The flavonoids in green tea are linked to heart and vascular health.

items.title: Calorie-free
items.content: Without sugar, green tea adds practically no calories.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: In large amounts, the caffeine in green tea can cause anxiety, insomnia, and a racing heartbeat.

items.title: Reduced iron absorption
items.content: Tea may reduce the absorption of iron from plant foods, so it is better to drink it between meals.

items.title: Extracts and the liver
items.content: Concentrated green tea supplements and extracts have in rare cases been linked to liver damage; discuss them with a doctor.

items.title: Medications and pregnancy
items.content: Green tea may affect how some medications work, and caffeine should be limited during pregnancy; consult a doctor if needed.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour water at about 70–80 °C over the leaves and steep for 1–3 minutes; boiling water and long steeping make the tea bitter. Whisk matcha powder with hot water using a whisk, or use it in smoothies, desserts, and baked goods. Green tea can also be enjoyed cold.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store green tea in an airtight container in a dark, dry, cool place away from light, moisture, and odors. It loses freshness faster than black tea, so use it within a few months. After opening, keep matcha in a tightly closed jar in the refrigerator.

vodka-sauce-with-tomatoes-and-cream.title: Vodka sauce with tomatoes and cream

content.title: About
content.content: Vodka sauce with tomatoes and cream is a classic Italian-inspired sauce where a tomato base is combined with the aromatic kick of vodka and the richness of cream. It is commonly served over pasta, especially penne or fettuccine. The vodka helps release the flavor of the tomatoes, while the cream gives the sauce a silky, smooth texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The “Vodka” sauce originated in the United States in the 1980s, though its roots trace back to Italian cuisine.
Vodka is used not for its alcohol content but to emulsify fats and enhance tomato flavor.
Traditional recipes call for only one to two tablespoons of vodka, but the amount can be adjusted to taste.
Cream used is usually 10‑30 % fat; higher‑fat cream yields a thicker sauce.
The sauce keeps well in the refrigerator for up to 3 days, but is best served freshly made.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Tomatoes provide lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health and skin.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Tomatoes contain vitamin C, which helps boost the immune system.

items.title: Contains calcium and vitamin D from cream
items.content: Cream adds calcium and a modest amount of vitamin D, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Moderate healthy fats
items.content: The cream contributes saturated and monounsaturated fats that can fit into a balanced diet.

items.title: Improves nutrient absorption
items.content: The small amount of alcohol enhances the bioavailability of certain tomato antioxidants.

items.title: Alcohol content
items.content: Although most alcohol evaporates during cooking, trace amounts may remain, which should be considered by those avoiding alcohol.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Cream and oil make the sauce calorie‑rich; portion control is advisable for weight‑managed diets.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cream contains lactose, so lactose‑intolerant individuals may opt for dairy‑free alternatives.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Tomato paste and pre‑made sauces can be salty; taste and adjust salt as needed.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Serve the sauce hot over pasta, rice, or vegetable dishes. It can be stirred into casseroles, used as a pizza base, or served as a dip with bread. For extra brightness, finish with fresh basil or grated Parmesan.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the sauce to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat gently on low heat, adding a splash of cream or water to restore its creamy consistency.
